# RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning

Shaopeng Fu Affiliation: KAUST    Xingxing Zhang Affiliation: Microsoft
Research    Li Dong Affiliation: Microsoft Research    Di Wang
Affiliation: KAUST    Furu Wei Affiliation: Microsoft Research

###### Abstract

While large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance
on complex reasoning tasks such as competitive programming (CP),
existing methods predominantly focus on single-attempt settings,
overlooking their capacity for iterative refinement. In this paper, we
present RefineRL, a novel approach designed to unleash the
self-refinement capabilities of LLMs for CP problem solving. RefineRL
introduces two key innovations: (1) Skeptical-Agent, an iterative
self-refinement agent equipped with local execution tools to validate
generated solutions against public test cases of CP problems. This agent
always maintains a skeptical attitude towards its own outputs and
thereby enforces rigorous self-refinement even when validation suggests
correctness. (2) A reinforcement learning (RL) solution to incentivize
LLMs to self-refine with only standard RLVR data (i.e., problems paired
with their verifiable answers). Extensive experiments on Qwen3-4B and
Qwen3-4B-2507 demonstrate that our method yields substantial gains:
after our RL training, these compact 4B models integrated with the
Skeptical-Agent not only outperform much larger 32B models but also
approach the single-attempt performance of 235B models. These findings
suggest that self-refinement holds considerable promise for scaling LLM
reasoning, with significant potential for further advancement.

###### Keywords: 

Machine Learning, ICML

## 1 Introduction

Recent large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong
mathematical reasoning capabilities in math competitions and competitive
programming (CP). Proprietary systems like OpenAI o1 ([El-Kishky et al.,
2025](#bib.bib23)), AlphaGeometry ([Trinh et al., 2024](#bib.bib28);
[Chervonyi et al., 2025](#bib.bib27)), and Gemini ([Comanici et al.,
2025](#bib.bib19)) have proven that reasoning LLMs can become medal
winners in the most challenging mind competitions. Concurrently,
open-source models like DeepSeek-R1 ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) and
Qwen3 ([Yang et al., 2025](#bib.bib11)) have achieved remarkable
performance on rigorous benchmarks such as AIME, LiveCodeBench, and
Codeforces. While the success of these models is largely attributed to
long Chain-of-thought (CoT; [Wei et al. 2022](#bib.bib29)) that can
consume tens of thousands of tokens during generations, the potential of
LLMs for iterative improvement remains under-explored. Indeed,
prevailing evaluations are performed in single-attempt settings, where
models are expected to derive correct solutions in a single inference
pass.

More recent studies have adopted the self-correction technique to
realize iterative improvement for competitive math proving ([Lin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib1); [Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)). In each turn, the
model utilizes the Lean-4 prover to analyze whether the generated proof
is incorrect, and if so, incorporates the feedback to correct the proof.
In the field of competitive programming, [Shi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib4)
and [Li et al. (2025)](#bib.bib31) represent the primary open-source
efforts leveraging self-correction. They employ Reflexion ([Shinn et
al., 2023](#bib.bib12)) to iteratively correct solutions until they pass
all public test cases. However, as public test cases serve only as a
sparse proxy for the comprehensive private test distribution, solely
relying on them to trigger iterative improvement introduces a risk of
false positives, where solutions pass visible checks but still fail on
unseen data. Furthermore, as a purely test-time method, Reflexion
depends entirely on the base model’s intrinsic iterative improvement
capabilities, lacking explicit training to optimize the improvement
process itself.

To address these challenges, we introduce RefineRL, a systematic
approach designed to unleash the latent reasoning capabilities of LLMs
for iterative improvement in competitive programming. Our framework is
built upon two core components: the Skeptical-Agent and Self-Refinement
Reinforcement Learning. Specifically, the Skeptical-Agent employs a
fine-grained agentic workflow tailored to different judging statuses on
public test cases of CP problems to perform the refinement. Unlike
previous approaches that blindly trust public validation, our agent
maintains a consistently skeptical attitude, enforcing rigorous
self-refinement even when passing all public test cases. However, this
self-refinement or self-skeptical capability either does not arise
naturally in LLMs or remains too weak to be effective. Therefore, we
propose Self-Refinement RL to explicitly incentivize this capability
with only standard RLVR data (i.e., problems paired with their
verifiable answers). By constructing a dataset solely from the model’s
own skeptical refinement trajectories and utilizing a new
squared-incentive reward function, we explicitly train LLMs to navigate
the complex self refinement process. Self-Refinement RL enables our
approach to go beyond static prompt engineering.

We evaluate RefineRL on two 4B reasoning LLMs, Qwen3-4B and
Qwen3-4B-2507. Results demonstrate that our method yields substantial
gains with high data efficiency: using only 4.5K problems from the
HardTest dataset ([He et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)) to construct training
samples, we significantly elevate the problem-solving capabilities of
compact 4B models. Notably, after Self-Refinement RL, RefineRL-4B and
RefineRL-4B-2507 equipped with the Skeptical-Agent not only outperform
the single-attempt performance of larger 32B models but also rival that
of significantly larger 235B models. These findings suggest that
self-refinement remains a largely under-explored avenue for scaling LLM
reasoning in competitive programming, holding significant potential for
further enhancement beyond model parameter scaling.

## 2 Related Work

Code generation of LLMs. Reasoning LLMs are found to be good at
generating program code with the help of long
chain-of-thought (CoT) ([Liu et al., 2024](#bib.bib18); [Yang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib11); [Comanici et al., 2025](#bib.bib19)). For competitive
programming, which is a specific code generation task, [Ahmad et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib20) show that training LLMs on long CoT data distilled
from frontier models can improve their capability to solve CP problems.
[He et al. (2025)](#bib.bib7), [Wang et al. (2025)](#bib.bib10), and [Fu
et al. (2025)](#bib.bib9) find that synthesized high-quality test cases
of CP problems boost RL training with verifiable rewards of LLMs. [Hu et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib21) further suggest using fully synthesized CP
problems to train LLMs. Despite model training, several test-time
scaling strategies such as example test cases rejection, longest
response selection, and clustering are also designed for the task of
solving CP problems ([El-Kishky et al., 2025](#bib.bib23); [Yu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Samadi et al., 2025](#bib.bib22)). Our work aims to
incentivize a new Skeptical-Agent capability for competitive programming
via RL training.

Self-correction of LLMs. Self-correction is a powerful test-time scaling
strategy that empowers LLMs to iteratively critique and improve their
responses based on internal or external feedback ([Shinn et al.,
2023](#bib.bib12); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib31); [Madaan et al.,
2023](#bib.bib30); [Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)). Previous works
have demonstrated its effectiveness for coding and mathematical
reasoning tasks ([Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); [Chen et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib14); [Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib15)), and recent studies
indicate that LLMs can further internalize this capability through
post-training ([Chen et al., 2024](#bib.bib13); [Jain et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib3); [Kumar et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)). However,
traditional approaches often rely on the complete history of multi-turn
interactions, leading to excessive context length that limits
practicality. More recent studies in competitive-level math
proving ([Zhou et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Lin et al., 2025](#bib.bib1);
[Shang et al., 2025](#bib.bib16); [Chen et al., 2025b](#bib.bib17))
suggest decomposing the correction process into multiple single-turn
feedback-response pairs, allowing the model to focus on immediate
corrections without retaining the full trajectory. This paradigm
significantly reduces computational overhead during both training and
inference. Our paper focuses on designing a self-refinement strategy
more robust than self-correction for solving CP problems and on
effectively using RL (post-)training to enhance such a capability.

## 3 Preliminaries

Competitive Programming (CP). A CP problem can be formalized as a triple
$`(x,T^{\text{pub}},T^{\text{pri}})`$, where $`x`$ is the problem
statement,
$`T^{\text{pub}}=\{(i^{\text{pub}}_{k},o^{\text{pub}}_{k})\}_{k=1}^{|T^{\text{pub}}|}`$
is the set of public test cases,
$`(i^{\text{pub}}_{k},o^{\text{pub}}_{k})`$ is the input-output pair of
the $`k`$-th public test case,
$`T^{\text{pri}}=\{(i^{\text{pri}}_{k},o^{\text{pri}}_{k})\}_{k=1}^{|T^{\text{pri}}|}`$
is the set of private test cases, and
$`(i^{\text{pri}}_{k},o^{\text{pri}}_{k})`$ is the input-output pair of
the $`k`$-th private test case. In a CP contest, the problem statement
$`x`$ and the public test cases $`T^{\text{pub}}`$ are visible to CP
contestants, while the private test cases $`T^{\text{pri}}`$ are not.
The goal of a CP contestant is to leverage all available information
from $`x`$ and $`T^{\text{pub}}`$ to write a code $`r_{\text{code}}`$
that solves the CP problem.

To determine whether the proposed solution code $`r_{\text{code}}`$
successfully solves the given problem
$`(x,T^{\text{pub}},T^{\text{pri}})`$, the contest coordinator will
leverage two oracle functions, i.e., an execution function
$`f(\cdot,\cdot)`$ and a judgment function $`g(\cdot,\cdot)`$, to
evaluate $`r_{\text{code}}`$ on the private test cases set
$`T^{\text{pri}}`$. Concretely, for the $`k`$-th private test case
$`(i^{\text{pri}}_{k},o^{\text{pri}}_{k})\in T^{\text{pri}}`$, one will
first use the execution function $`f(\cdot,\cdot)`$ to run the code
$`r_{\text{code}}`$ on the private test input $`i^{\text{pri}}_{k}`$ as
follows,

|     |                                                                                  |     |     |
| --- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle\hat{o}^{\text{pri}}_{k}=f(r_{\text{code}},i^{\text{pri}}_{k}),`$ |     | (1) |

where $`\hat{o}^{\text{pri}}_{k}`$ is the execution output. Then,
$`\hat{o}^{\text{pri}}_{k}`$ will be compared with the private test
output $`o^{\text{pri}}_{k}`$ using the judgment function
$`g(\cdot,\cdot)`$ as follows,

|     |                                                                                      |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle j^{\text{pri}}_{k}=g(\hat{o}^{\text{pri}}_{k},o^{\text{pri}}_{k}),`$ |     | (2) |

where $`j^{\text{pri}}_{k}`$ is the judging status, indicating whether
the code $`r_{\text{code}}`$ passes the test case
$`(i^{\text{pri}}_{k},o^{\text{pri}}_{k})`$ and, if it fails, the
failure reason. In this paper, we adopt six judging statuses commonly
found in real-world CP contests, which are: “Accepted (AC)”, “Wrong
Answer (WA)”, “Time Limit Exceeded (TLE)”, “Memory Limit Exceeded
(MLE)”, “Compile Error (CE)”, and “Runtime Error (RE)”. Among them, “AC”
indicates that the code passes the given test case, while “WA”, “TLE”,
“MLE”, “CE”, and “RE” explain why the code fails on the given test case.

Finally, the proposed solution code $`x_{\text{code}}`$ is determined to
successfully solve the given problem
$`(x,T^{\text{pub}},T^{\text{pri}})`$ if it passes all private test
cases of the problem. In other words, $`x_{\text{code}}`$ is considered
to be correct if and only if the following indicator function outputs
one,

|     |                                            |                |
| --- | ------------------------------------------ | -------------- | --------------------------------------- | -------------- | --------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle 1\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum\_{k=1}^{ | T^{\text{pri}} | }1[j^{\text{pri}}_{k}=\text{AC}]\Bigr)= | T^{\text{pri}} | \Bigr],`$ |     |

where
$`j^{\text{pri}}_{k}=g(f(r_{\text{code}},i^{\text{pri}}_{k}),o^{\text{pri}}_{k})`$
for every $`1\leq k\leq|T^{\text{pri}}|`$.

Solving CP problems with LLMs. Let $`\pi_{\theta}`$ be a reasoning LLM
parameterized by $`\theta`$. Then, for a given CP problem
$`(x,T^{\text{pub}},T^{\text{pri}})`$, one can directly prompt the LLM
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ to solve the problem as follows,

|     |                                                                                      |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle(r_{\text{cot}},r_{\text{sol}},r_{\text{code}})\sim\pi_{\theta}(x),`$ |     | (3) |

where $`r_{\text{sol}}`$ is the generated CoT, $`r_{\text{sol}}`$ is the
generated text solution, and $`r_{\text{code}}`$ is the solution code
(e.g., Python code) corresponding to the text solution. In this paper,
we focus on generating Python solutions, and the prompt template that we
use for
Eq. ([3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))
is presented in
Figure [4](#A3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").

## 4 RefineRL

This section presents our RefineRL approach for competitive programming.
We will first motivate the necessity of integrating skepticism into
iterative improvement-based CP problem solving, and then introduce our
proposed Skeptical-Agent and Self-Refinement RL in detail.

### 4.1 Motivation

In the domain of competitive programming, [Shi et al. (2024)](#bib.bib4)
and [Li et al. (2025)](#bib.bib31) are primary open-source efforts
leveraging self-correction for iterative improvement. In their approach,
the model analyzes the improvement history and iteratively corrects its
generated code until the solution passes all visible public test cases
or reaches the maximum steps. However, public test cases are usually
sparse and weak, failing to cover the comprehensive distribution of
private test cases, particularly edge cases. This limitation creates a
significant risk of false positives: a solution passing all visible
public test cases can still fail on unseen private ones.

To tackle false positives, we argue that a necessary and promising
approach is to integrate skepticism into the iterative improvement
process for competitive programming. The LLM should not blindly trust
evaluations on public test cases but rather maintain a skeptical
attitude, continuing refinement even when public evaluations suggest
correctness. Built upon this principle, our Skeptical-Agent utilizes
specialized prompts to enforce persistent self-refinement, while
Self-Refinement RL internalizes this self-refinement capability through
post-training, enabling the LLM to discover and resolve defects beyond
public test cases.

### 4.2 Skeptical-Agent

Given a CP problem $`(x,T^{\text{pub}},T^{\text{pri}})`$, the
Skeptical-Agent will try to propose and iteratively improve solutions
for up to $`N`$ iterations solely based on the problem statement $`x`$
and the public test case set $`T^{\text{pub}}`$. In each iteration,
following a design similar to that in [Kumar et al. (2025)](#bib.bib8),
[Jain et al. (2025a)](#bib.bib3), and [Lin et al. (2025)](#bib.bib1),
our Skeptical-Agent will use at most the information from the last
solution attempt to construct feedback to improve this time’s
generation.

Self-refinement in Skeptical-Agent. Concretely, suppose
$`(r^{(n)}_{\text{cot}},r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n)}_{\text{code}})`$ is
the solution tuple generated in the $`n`$-th refinement iteration. To
construct a feedback $`r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}`$ from it for the
$`(n+1)`$-th generation, we sequentially evaluate the generated code
$`r^{(n)}_{\text{code}}`$ on each public test case from the set
$`T^{\text{pub}}`$. For the $`k`$-th public test case
$`(i^{\text{pub}}_{k},o^{\text{pub}}_{k})`$, we first obtaining an
execution output
$`\hat{o}^{(n)}_{k}:=f(r^{(n)}_{\text{code}},i^{\text{pub}}_{k})`$ (see
Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")))
and then calculating a judging status
$`j^{(n)}_{k}:=g(\hat{o}^{(n)}_{k},o^{\text{pub}}_{k})`$, using the
oracle execution and judgment functions $`f`$ and $`g`$ respectively.
Finally, the $`(n+1)`$-th solution generation process of Skeptical-Agent
is formalized as follows,

|     |                                                                                                                                   |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle(r^{(n+1)}_{\text{cot}},r^{(n+1)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n+1)}_{\text{code}})\sim\pi_{\theta}(x,r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}),`$ |     | (4) |

where $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is the reasoning LLM and $`r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}`$
is the $`n`$-th feedback constructed from the evaluation of the $`n`$-th
generated solution on the public test cases set $`T^{\text{pub}}`$. The
prompt template used by
Eq. ([4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))
is presented in
Figure [4](#A3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").

Then, to maintain skepticism, the Skeptical-Agent will use one of the
Failure-driven feedback and skepticism-driven feedback during
refinement, detailed as follows.

Failure-driven feedback. During the sequential evaluation, if the
solution code fails to pass the $`k`$-th public test case, i.e., if
$`j^{(n)}_{k}\in\{\text{WA},\text{TLE},\text{MLE},\text{CE},\text{RE}\}`$,
then the evaluation will be terminated and the feedback
$`r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}`$ obtained from the $`n`$-th generation is
constructed as follows:

|     |                                                                                                                                                                                   |     |     |
| --- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}=\mathcal{P}_{\text{Fail}}(r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n)}_{\text{code}},i^{\text{pub}}_{k},o^{\text{pub}}_{k},\hat{o}^{(n)}_{k},j^{(n)}_{k}),`$ |     | (5) |

where $`\mathcal{P}_{\text{Fail}}`$ is the failure-feedback function
that constructs feedback prompts for different failed judging statuses
$`j^{(n)}_{k}`$ with different failure reason explanations. The prompt
template for $`\mathcal{P}_{\text{Fail}}`$ and the failure reason
explanation template are in
Figure [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
and
Figure [6](#A3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").
This design aims to provide as many failure details as possible,
including a failed test case, the execution result, and a detailed
failure explanation, to assist the LLM to generate better solutions.

Skepticism-driven feedback. If the solution code
$`r^{(n)}_{\text{code}}`$ successfully passes all public test cases,
i.e., if $`j^{(n)}_{k}=\text{AC}`$ for every
$`(i^{\text{pub}}_{k},o^{\text{pub}}_{k})\in T^{\text{pub}}`$, there
might still be bugs or wrong ideas in the solution that can cause the
code to fail in edge or extreme private test cases from
$`T^{\text{pri}}`$. However, in this setting, there is no test case that
can be used for the feedback and assisting the next-time solution
generation in FaSC. To tackle such a challenge, we propose to instead
construct the feedback solely using the generated solution text
$`r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}}`$ and code $`r^{(n)}_{\text{code}}`$ as follows,

|     |                                                                                                               |     |     |
| --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}=\mathcal{P}_{\text{Skep}}(r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n)}_{\text{code}}),`$ |     | (6) |

where $`\mathcal{P}_{\text{Skep}}`$ is the Skepticism-feedback function
that constructs prompts to ask the LLM itself to re-check the generated
solution $`(r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n)}_{\text{code}})`$. The prompt
template for $`\mathcal{P}_{\text{Skep}}`$ is presented in
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
in
Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
focusing on checking: (1) whether $`r^{(n)}_{\text{code}}`$ encodes
public test cases as short-cuts, (2) whether
$`(r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n)}_{\text{code}})`$ is correct, and
(3) whether the time and space complexities of
$`(r^{(n)}_{\text{sol}},r^{(n)}_{\text{code}})`$ are optimal.

Algorithm 1 Skeptical-Agent for CP Problem Solving

Overall agent-loop workflow. As aforementioned, in the agent-loop
workflow, the Skeptical Agent performs up to $`N`$ self-refinement
iterations. We further adopt the following two additional rules, with
two additional hyperparameters $`M_{1}`$ and $`M_{2}`$, to control the
workflow:

- •
  Restart Rule. If the agent fails to generate a solution that passes
  all test cases in $`T^{\text{pub}}`$ for $`M_{1}`$ consecutive
  attempts, then in the $`(M_{1}+1)`$-th trial, it will discard the
  feedback from the previous attempt and generate a solution solely
  based on the problem statement $`x`$.
- •
  Termination Rule. If the agent generates solutions that pass all test
  cases in $`T^{\text{pub}}`$ for $`M_{2}`$ consecutive attempts, it
  will terminate the refinement process and select the last attempt as
  the final solution.

The Restart Rule is designed to prevent the self-refinement process from
getting trapped in local optima. Conversely, the Termination Rule
compels the LLM to re-examine and rectify potential latent bugs in the
proposed solution, even when it already satisfies all public test cases.
Putting all these components together, the overall algorithm of the
Skeptical Agent is presented as
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").

### 4.3 Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning

We now detail our Self-Refinement RL for improving the self-refinement
capability of the Skeptical-Agent. We use the GRPO ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)) algorithm, excluding KL-regularization, to perform RL
training. The objective function for training an LLM $`\pi_{\theta}`$ is
formalized as follows,

|     |     |                                                                                                                                            |       |
| --- | --- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | ----- | --- |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\E_{q\sim D,\{o*{i}\}*{i=1}^{G}\sim\pi*{\theta*{\text{old}}}(\cdot                        | q)}`$ |     |
|     |     | $`\displaystyle\frac{1}{G}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\min\Bigl(s_{i}\hat{A}_{i},\text{clip}\left(s_{i},1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)\hat{A}_{i}\Bigr),`$ |       |

where $`q`$ is the input sample drawn from the training set $`D`$,
$`\{o_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ is the group of responses,
$`s_{i}:=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(o_{i}|q)}{\pi_{\theta_{\text{old}}}(o_{i}|q)}`$
is the importance sampling ratio,
$`\hat{A}_{i}:=\frac{R_{i}-\text{mean}(R)}{\text{std}(R)}`$ is the
advantage for the $`i`$-th response, and $`\{R_{i}\}_{i=1}^{G}`$ is the
group of rewards for each response.

To help internalize the skeptical self-refinement capability, our
Skeptical RL also adopts two unique designs: (1) a novel RL training
data synthesis paradigm, and (2) a new reward function for better RL
training on CP problems.

RL training data synthesis. From the solution generation process
formalized in
Eq. ([4](#S4.E4 "Equation 4 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))
in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
the key to advancing the Skeptical-Agent is to train LLMs to better
perform self-refinement with the feedback $`r^{(n)}_{\text{fed}}`$ that
can be either error-driven feedback (see
Eq. ([5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")))
or skepticism-driven feedback (see
Eq. ([6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))).
To this end, in our Self-Refinement RL, for a reasoning LLM
$`\pi_{\theta}`$, we propose to construct, from a normal CP problem
dataset, a training dataset that contains prompts combined with
failure/skepticism-feedback synthesized solely based on the LLM
$`\pi_{\theta}`$ itself.

Concretely, suppose $`D_{\text{CP}}:=\{(x_{q},T_{q})\}_{q=1}^{|D|}`$ is
a CP problem dataset where $`x_{q}`$ is the statement of the $`q`$-th
problem and $`T_{q}`$ is the corresponding test cases set mixing of both
public and private test cases. We use the LLM $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to
construct two new self-refinement datasets,
$`D_{\text{Err}}:=\{(x_{q},r^{\text{Err}}_{\text{fed},q},T_{q})\}_{q=1}^{|D^{\text{Err}}|}`$
and
$`D_{\text{Skep}}:=\{(x_{q},r^{\text{Skep}}_{\text{fed},q},T_{q})\}_{q=1}^{|D^{\text{Skep}}|}`$,
where $`r^{\text{Err}}_{\text{fed},q}`$ is the error-driven feedback
from
Eq. ([5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))
and $`r^{\text{Skep}}_{\text{fed},q}`$ is the skepticism-driven feedback
from
Eq. ([6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")).
The eventual Self-Refinement RL training dataset $`D_{\text{RL}}`$ is
formalized as the union of the original and self-refinement data, i.e.,
$`D_{\text{RL}}:=D_{\text{CP}}\cup D_{\text{Err}}\cup D_{\text{Skep}}`$.
During training, for each tuple $`(x,r_{\text{fed}},T)`$ from the set
$`D_{\text{RL}}`$, we use the prompt template in
Figure [4](#A3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
to construct the actual prompt for performing the rollout process of RL.

The construction of the two self-refinement datasets, $`D_{\text{Err}}`$
and $`D_{\text{Skep}}`$, is detailed as follows:

- •
  Failure-feedback set $`D_{\text{Err}}`$. For each tuple
  $`(x_{q},T_{q})\in D_{\text{CP}}`$ from the original CP problem set,
  we first use the LLM $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to generate solution text
  $`x_{\text{sol},q}`$ and code $`x_{\text{code},q}`$ following
  Eq. ([3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")),
  and evaluate the code $`x_{\text{code},q}`$ on the test case set
  $`T_{q}`$ using the execution and judging functions $`f`$ and $`g`$ in
  Eq. ([1](#S3.E1 "Equation 1 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))
  and
  Eq. ([2](#S3.E2 "Equation 2 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")).
  If $`x_{\text{code},q}`$ successfully passes all test cases from
  $`T_{q}`$, then we will exclude this CP problem from the
  failure-feedback set construction. Otherwise, if $`x_{\text{code},q}`$
  fails on the test case $`(i_{q,k},o_{q,k})\in T_{q}`$, we will record
  its corresponding execution output
  $`\hat{o}_{q,k}:=f(r_{\text{code},q},i_{q,k})`$ and judging status
  $`j_{q,k}:=g(\hat{o}_{q,k},o_{q,k})`$. The error-driven feedback for
  problem $`(x_{q},T_{q})`$ is then constructed as
  $`r^{\text{Err}}_{\text{fed},q}:=\mathcal{P}_{\text{Fail}}(r_{\text{sol},q},r_{\text{code},q},i_{q,k},o_{q,k},\hat{o}_{q,k},j_{q,k})`$
  following
  Eq. ([5](#S4.E5 "Equation 5 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")).
  The constructed tuple $`(x_{q},r^{\text{Err}}_{\text{fed},q},T_{q})`$
  will be added to the failure-feedback set $`D_{\text{Err}}`$.
- •
  Skepticism-feedback set $`D_{\text{Skep}}`$. For each tuple
  $`(x_{q},T_{q})\in D_{\text{CP}}`$ from the original CP problem set,
  we similarly use the LLM $`\pi_{\theta}`$ to generate solution text
  $`x_{\text{sol},q}`$ and code $`x_{\text{code},q}`$. Then, without
  knowing whether the generated code $`r_{\text{code},q}`$ can pass the
  test case set $`T_{q}`$, we directly construct a skepticism-feedback
  for this problem as
  $`r^{\text{Skep}}_{\text{fed},q}:=\mathcal{P}_{\text{Skep}}(r_{\text{sol},q},r_{\text{code},q})`$
  following
  Eq. ([6](#S4.E6 "Equation 6 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")).
  Finally, for the constructed triple
  $`(x_{q},r^{\text{Skep}}_{\text{fed},q},T_{q})`$, if
  $`r_{\text{code},q}`$ successfully passes all test cases from the set
  $`T_{q}`$, then the tuple will be added to the new skepticism-feedback
  set $`D_{\text{Skep}}`$ with a probability of $`20\%`$. Otherwise,
  i.e., if $`r_{\text{code},q}`$ fails any test case from $`T_{q}`$,
  then the probability of adding
  $`(x_{q},r^{\text{Skep}}_{\text{fed},q},T_{q})`$ to
  $`D_{\text{Skep}}`$ will be $`40\%`$.

Squared-incentive reward. Existing studies of RL training on CP problems
usually use a pass-or-fail reward function where a generated solution
code $`x_{\text{code}}`$ receives a non-trivial reward from a CP problem
$`(x,T)`$ if and only if it passes all test cases from the set
$`T`$ ([He et al., 2025](#bib.bib7); [Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)).
While such a pass-or-fail reward is close to settings of real-world CP
contests such as CodeForces or ICPC where contestants need to pass all
test cases to get scores from a single problem, we note that it may
hinder RL training. Specifically, for a given CP problem $`(x,T)`$, if
it is so difficult that the LLM being trained cannot generate any
correct solution to pass the test case set $`T`$, then the LLM cannot
obtain any non-trivial reward and thus cannot learn anything from
$`(x,T)`$.

To address this technical challenge, our Skeptical RL training adopt a
new Squared-incentive Reward function that is specifically designed for
RL training on CP data. Given a CP problem $`(x,T)`$ and a generated
solution code $`r_{\text{code}}`$, the squared-incentive reward for
$`r_{\text{code}}`$ is calculated as follows,

|     |                                                 |     |
| --- | ----------------------------------------------- | --- | -------- | --- |
|     | $`\displaystyle R(r\_{\text{code}},T):=(k^{\*}/ | T   | )^{2},`$ |     |

where $`k^{*}`$ is equal to either $`|T|`$ or the index minus one of the
first test case from the set $`T`$ that $`r_{\text{code}}`$ fails to
pass. The advantage of our new squared-incentive reward is two-fold:

- •
  It enables the LLM to extract meaningful learning signals from
  difficult CP problems even though the LLM itself cannot roll out a
  correct solution during RL.
- •
  It incentivizes the LLM to completely solve CP problems as the squared
  nature of the reward significantly amplifies the total reward for
  passing later test cases.

## 5 Experiments

This section presents experiments on our RefineRL. We will empirically
evaluate our Skeptical-Agent and how our Self-Refinement RL can advance
its performance.

### 5.1 Experimental Setup

Test-time scaling and baselines. For our proposed Skeptical Agent in
Algorithm [1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 4.2 Skeptical-Agent ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
we denote it as Skeptical@16 and set its query budget $`N`$ to 16 and
the remaining two hyperparameters $`M_{1}`$ and $`M_{2}`$ to 4 and 8
respectively.

Besides, we adopt the following five baseline test-time scaling
strategies: (1) Pass@1: Directly querying the LLM once using
Eq. ([3](#S3.E3 "Equation 3 ‣ 3 Preliminaries ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"))
and extracting solutions from its response. (2) Random@16: Generating 16
responses in parallel and random choose one that passes all public test
cases. (3) LongCoT@16: Generating 16 responses in parallel and random
choose one that passes all public test cases and has the longest CoT
length. (4) RejSamp@16: Repeatedly querying the LLM up to 16 times until
a solution code that can pass all public test cases is generated.
(5) Reflexion@16 ([Shi et al., 2024](#bib.bib4)): Repeatedly querying
the LLM up to 16 times with the full historical generation results until
a solution code that can pass the problem is generated. Note that
Random@16 and LongCoT@16 are parallel sampling-based baselines, while
RejSamp@16 and Reflexion@16 are sequential sampling-based baselines.

Training data of RL. We select 4.5K CP problems from the HardTest
dataset ([He et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)) that are suitable for learning
self-refinement to form the base problem set $`D_{\text{CP}}`$. We then
follow the pipeline described in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
to construct the final Self-Refinement RL training data. Specifically,
we set the maximum generation length to 32,768 for Qwen3-4B and 65,536
for Qwen3-4B-2507, resulting in approximately 4.2K self-refinement
trajectories for each model. Please see
Appendix [A.1](#A1.SS1 "A.1 Training Data for Self-Refinement RL ‣ Appendix A Additional Implementation Details ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
for full details.

RL training. We perform RL training via GRPO ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib6)) on two 4B LLMs, Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-4B-2507 ([Yang et
al., 2025](#bib.bib11)). The maximum rollout generation token length
during RL is set to 32,768 for Qwen3-4B and 65,536 for Qwen3-4B-2507.
The two RL trained models from Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-4B-2507 are denoted as
RefineRL-4B and RefineRL-4B-2507, respectively. Please refer to
Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 RL Training Details ‣ Appendix A Additional Implementation Details ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
for full details about RL hyperparameters and the implementation of
efficient reward calculation.

Evaluations. We use two versions of LiveCodeBench ([Jain et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib26)), v5 (2024.10-2025.01; 167 problems) and
v6 (2025.01-2025.03; 175 problems), to evaluate the capability of LLMs
in solving CP problems. In every LLM for evaluation, we set the the
sampling temperature and top-$`p`$ to 0.6 and 0.95, respectively. For
the max generation token length, we set 32,768 for Qwen3-4B and
RefineRL-4B and 65,536 for all other models. To ensure a fair
comparison, all models are evaluated using our self-implemented
evaluation toolkit. Plese refer to
Appendix [A.3](#A1.SS3 "A.3 Evaluation Details ‣ Appendix A Additional Implementation Details ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
for details.

### 5.2 Results Analysis

We present the RL training logs in
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B Additional Experimental Results ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").
Here, we focus on analyzing the CP problem-solving performance gains by
the Skeptical-Agent and Self-Refinement RL.

Comparison with baseline models. We first compare the performance of our
RefineRL-4B and RefineRL-4B-2507 models against other strong baselines
in
Table [1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.3 Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").
From the table, we observe two key findings: Firstly, while
Self-Refinement RL is primarily designed to enhance the self-refinement
capability of LLMs, it also significantly boosts standard Pass@1
performance. For instance, it enables the RefineRL-4B to achieve
performance comparable to 8B models (e.g., Qwen3-8B), while the
RefineRL-4B-2507 rivals 32B models (e.g., OCR-Nemotron-1.1-32B).
Secondly, when equipped with our inference-time strategy,
Skeptical-Agent (i.e., Skeptical@16), our RefineCoder-4B-2507
outperforms 32B baselines and closely approaches the much larger
Qwen3-235B-A22B-2507, narrowing the performance gap to less than 5% on
both LiveCodeBench v5 and v6. All these results demonstrate that our
approach effectively unleash the self-refinement capabilities of LLMs,
allowing compact 4B models to achieve state-of-the-art performance
through efficient training and inference strategies.

Comparison with inference-time baselines. We then evaluate our
Skeptical-Agent (i.e., Skeptical@16) against various test-time scaling
baselines on both base and post-trained models, as detailed in
Table [2](#S4.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 4.3 Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").
Firstly, we compare against parallel sampling baselines (i.e., Random@16
and LongCoT@16). Our Skeptical-Agent consistently outperforms both
(e.g., improving RefineRL-4B-2507 from 64.14% to 67.82% on
LiveCodeBench v6), demonstrating that simply scaling up test-time
compute via parallel generation—even when heuristically selecting for
deeper reasoning—is less effective than our targeted, iterative
refinement strategy. Secondly, we evaluate against sequential baselines
(i.e., RejSamp@16 and Reflexion@16) to rigorously isolate the source of
our gains. Crucially, our method outperforms RejSamp@16, which
effectively refutes the concern that our improvements stem merely from
stochastic re-sampling, as RejSamp also maximizes the sampling budget to
pass public tests. Furthermore, by surpassing Reflexion@16, which tends
to prematurely accept false positives, we validate that the performance
boost stems directly from our skepticism-driven feedback, which enables
the agent to uncover and rectify latent bugs that pass public test
cases.

Effect of RL training on model responses. Finally, we analyze the
behavioral changes induced by our Self-Refinement RL, as shown in
Table [3](#S5.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 5.2 Results Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").
We observe that while the average number of self-refinement rounds
slightly decreases after RL training, the average response length
significantly increases. This suggests that our Self-Refinement RL
objective does not merely incentivize the model to “try more times”
(which would increase the round count), but rather to “think deeper”
within each attempt. By generating longer and more detailed CoT, the
model effectively trades the quantity of attempts for the quality of
reasoning. Crucially, this substantial increase in reasoning length for
RefineRL-4B-2507 correlates with the superior performance gains reported
in our main results, reinforcing the hypothesis that extended,
comprehensive CoT is instrumental in solving complex CP problems.

| Qwen3-4B                | 10.38              | 10,297.97            |
| RefineRL-4B (Ours)      | 9.78               | 11,371.62            |
| Qwen3-4B-2507           | 9.26               | 10,330.52            |
| RefineRL-4B-2507 (Ours) | 8.66               | 17,558.65            |

### 5.3 Ablation Studies

Effect of self-refinement trajectory data. We now investigate whether
the performance gains observed in our self-refinement RL are primarily
driven by the use of self-generated refinement trajectory data. We train
additional baseline models (denoted as “Standard RL”) solely on the
original base set of 4.5K CP problems from HardTest. To ensure a fair
comparison, these baselines employ the same squared-incentive reward
function as our Self-Refinement RL. The results, summarized in
Table [4](#S5.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 5.2 Results Analysis ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
demonstrate that models trained with self-refinement trajectories
consistently outperform the Standard RL baselines. Furthermore, this
performance gain is observed not only in the Skeptical-Agent setting but
also in the single-attempt generation setting (i.e., Pass@1). This
suggests that exposing the model to the full refinement process enables
it to internalize the debugging capability, yielding superior reasoning
performance compared to learning from problem statements alone.

| Model & Strategy                                | LCB-v5 | LCB-v6 |
| ----------------------------------------------- | ------ | ------ |
| Qwen3-4B                                        | 52.51  | 48.29  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Pass-or-fail Reward      | 51.35  | 47.04  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Squared-incentive Reward | 56.40  | 48.79  |
| Qwen3-4B + Skeptical@16                         | 62.13  | 56.18  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Pass-or-fail Reward      | 62.05  | 55.50  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Squared-incentive Reward | 64.07  | 56.54  |
| Qwen3-4B-2507                                   | 62.65  | 55.21  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Pass-or-fail Reward      | 64.22  | 55.36  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Squared-incentive Reward | 70.40  | 61.57  |
| Qwen3-4B-2507 + Skeptical@16                    | 71.29  | 62.07  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Pass-or-fail Reward      | 70.55  | 61.43  |
| + Self-Refinement RL + Squared-incentive Reward | 75.97  | 67.82  |

Table 5: Performance of models trained via Skeptical-RL with the
original squared-incentive reward or pass-or-fail reward.

Effect of squared-incentive reward. We next investigate the efficacy of
our squared-incentive reward by comparing it with the traditional binary
pass-or-fail reward (i.e., assigning a reward of 1 if all tests pass,
and 0 otherwise) commonly used in code RL. To ensure a controlled
comparison, we train baselines using the binary reward while keeping the
self-refinement trajectory data fixed. The results in
Table [5](#S5.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 5.3 Ablation Studies ‣ 5 Experiments ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
reveal a stark contrast: while binary rewards fail to yield consistent
improvements and even degrade performance, our squared-incentive reward
delivers robust gains across all settings. This indicates that the
dense, fine-grained feedback provided by our design is essential for
complex CP tasks, whereas sparse binary signals often fail to provide
sufficient guidance for stable policy improvement.

## 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we propose RefineRL, an approach designed to incentivize
the self-refinement capabilities of LLMs for competitive programming. To
address the unreliability of public test cases, we first introduce the
Skeptical-Agent, which maintains a persistent attitude of skepticism
toward its generated solutions. By enforcing rigorous self-refinement
even when local evaluations suggest correctness, this agent effectively
mitigates the risk of blindly trusting sparse public test cases.
Complementing this, we further propose Self-Refinement RL, a training
pipeline that internalizes this “doubt and debug” capability via
self-generated refinement trajectories and a novel squared-incentive
reward. Empirically, we demonstrate that RefineRL enables compact 4B
models to outperform the single-attempt performance of 32B baselines and
rival that of much larger 235B models. These results suggest that
explicit training for intrinsic self-refinement is a far more data- and
parameter-efficient path toward achieving advanced reasoning
intelligence.

## Appendix A Additional Implementation Details

### A.1 Training Data for Self-Refinement RL

We construct the training dataset for Skeptical RL based on a subset of
the HardTest dataset ([He et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)), consisting of CP
problems that are suitable for learning self-refinement. Formally, a
problem is considered to be suitable if it contains at least 8 test
cases with both input and output lengths not exceeding 512 tokens. The
idea behind this is that short input-output pairs are essential for both
humans and AI models to effectively diagnose errors and facilitate
debugging.

To form the base CP problem dataset $`D_{\text{CP}}`$, we select
suitable problems from the first 1/8 of HardTest. For each selected
problem, we retain all test cases shorter than 512 tokens and randomly
sample up to 8 additional test cases from the remainder. This process
results in a base set $`D_{\text{CP}}`$ consisting of approximately 4.5K
CP problems.

Finally, we employ the pipeline described in
Section [4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning ‣ 4 RefineRL ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
to synthesize the final Self-Refinement RL training data. We focus on
generating Python code, and set the maximum generation length to 32,768
for Qwen3-4B and 65,536 for Qwen3-4B-2507. For each model, this process
generates approximately 4.2K self-refinement trajectories. Combining
these with the base problems yields a total of roughly 8.7K training
samples per model. Detailed statistics of the final training datasets
are presented in
Table [6](#A1.T6 "Table 6 ‣ A.1 Training Data for Self-Refinement RL ‣ Appendix A Additional Implementation Details ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").

|                                                  |          |               |
| ------------------------------------------------ | -------- | ------------- |
| Data Type                                        | Qwen3-4B | Qwen3-4B-2507 |
| Initial CP Problems from $`D_{\text{CP}}`$       | 4,500    | 4,500         |
| Error-driven Trajectory                          | 2,811    | 2,721         |
|    \[True Negative\] Wrong Answer (WA)           | 2,127    | 2,077         |
|    \[True Negative\] Runtime Error (RE)          | 377      | 364           |
|    \[True Negative\] Time Limit Exceeded (TLE)   | 307      | 280           |
|    \[True Negative\] Compile Error (CE)          | 0        | 0             |
|    \[True Negative\] Memory Limit Exceeded (MLE) | 0        | 0             |
| Skepticism-driven Trajectory                     | 1,449    | 1,471         |
|    \[True Positive\] Accepted (AC)               | 309      | 370           |
|    \[False Positive\] AC $`\rightarrow`$ WA      | 863      | 856           |
|    \[False Positive\] AC $`\rightarrow`$ RE      | 148      | 139           |
|    \[False Positive\] AC $`\rightarrow`$ TLE     | 129      | 106           |
|    \[False Positive\] AC $`\rightarrow`$ CE      | 0        | 0             |
|    \[False Positive\] AC $`\rightarrow`$ MLE     | 0        | 0             |

“WA/RE/TLE/CE/MLE” represent trajectories triggered by error-driven
feedback. “AC $`\rightarrow`$ WA/RE/TLE/CE/MLE” denote trajectories
involving skepticism-driven feedback, where the solution passed public
test cases but failed on private ones due to the indicated errors.

### A.2 RL Training Details

We use the VeRL framework ¹¹ 1
[https://github.com/volcengine/verl](https://github.com/volcengine/verl) ([Sheng
et al., 2024](#bib.bib25)) to perform RL training via the GRPO ([Guo et
al., 2025](#bib.bib6)) algorithm, where the KL-regularization term is
excluded. both the batch size and mini-batch size are set to 32 and For
the rollout hyperparameters of GRPO, we set the rollout number to 8, the
maximum response length to 32,768 for Qwen3-4B and 65,536 for
Qwen3-4B-2507, the temperature to 1.0, and the top-$`p`$ to 1.0. AdamW
is adopted as the optimizer, where the learning rate is fixed to
$`10^{-6}`$ throughout the RL training. The two RL trained models from
Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-4B-2507 are denoted as RefineRL-4B and
RefineRL-4B-2507, respectively.

Calculating rewards for CP data requires executing LLM-generated code
against multiple private test cases, which is a CPU-intensive process.
To enable efficient and scalable reward computation during RL training,
we integrate our evaluation logic with the VeRL framework, which is
built upon the distributed computing engine Ray ²² 2
[https://github.com/ray-project/ray](https://github.com/ray-project/ray).
We leverage Ray to schedule distributed code evaluations, assigning
isolated CPU cores for individual execution tasks. To strictly manage
resource consumption during training, we employ timeout ³³ 3
[https://man.archlinux.org/man/timeout.1](https://man.archlinux.org/man/timeout.1)
and prlimit ⁴⁴ 4
[https://man.archlinux.org/man/prlimit.1](https://man.archlinux.org/man/prlimit.1)
to enforce time and memory constraints, set to 8 seconds and 512MB,
respectively. Finally, to ensure reasoning integrity, we enforce
complete CoT generation: only responses containing the CoT closing
delimiter (i.e., the \</think\> tag) are submitted for reward
calculation; otherwise, a reward of 0 is assigned.

### A.3 Evaluation Details

Existing evaluations on the LiveCodeBench benchmark typically rely on
the official LCB evaluation toolkit ⁵⁵ 5
[https://github.com/LiveCodeBench/LiveCodeBench](https://github.com/LiveCodeBench/LiveCodeBench)
or the Hugging Face LightEval package ⁶⁶ 6
[https://github.com/huggingface/lighteval](https://github.com/huggingface/lighteval).
However, we argue that these packages are inefficient for large-scale CP
solution judging, as they lack native support for high-throughput
parallel inference and fail to fully leverage multi-core CPUs for
computationally intensive solution code execution. To address these
limitations, we implemented a custom, scalable toolkit for efficient CP
performance evaluation.

Our implementation decouples the evaluation pipeline into two distinct
stages to ensure robustness and efficiency:

- •
  Step 1: LLM solution generation. We utilize the SGLang inference
  engine ⁷⁷ 7
  [https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang](https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang)
  to perform high-throughput parallel LLM generation. We adopt the
  standard LiveCodeBench solution generation prompts from the LightEval
  package for LLMs to generate Python solutions, with the exception of
  our Skeptical-Agent, which incorporates the additional feedback
  prompts detailed in
  Appendix [C](#A3 "Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
  to perform self-refinement.
- •
  Step 2: Concurrent code evaluation. Consistent with the training setup
  described in
  Appendix [A.2](#A1.SS2 "A.2 RL Training Details ‣ Appendix A Additional Implementation Details ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
  we employ the Unix CLI tools timeout and prlimit to enforce strict
  time and memory constraints. To maximize resource utilization, we
  leverage native multiprocessing for the Python’s asyncio ⁸⁸ 8
  [https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html](https://docs.python.org/3/library/asyncio.html)
  package to evaluate multiple solutions concurrently.

Regarding evaluation settings, for every CP problem, we set a time limit
of 6s and a memory limit of 512MB. All code executions are performed on
a 2.5GHz multi-core CPU. To ensure a fair comparison, all models in our
experiments are evaluated using our custom toolkit, with results
averaged over 16 runs to ensure stability. The LLM sampling parameters
are set to a temperature of 0.6 and a top-$`p`$ of 0.95. The maximum
generation length is set to 32,768 tokens for Qwen3-4B and our
RefineRL-4B, and 65,536 tokens for all other models. Furthermore, given
that the evaluated models are reasoning-oriented, we strictly enforce
complete Chain-of-Thought (CoT) integrity; specifically, only responses
containing a detected CoT completion tag are submitted for evaluation;
otherwise, they are assigned a score of zero.

Across both models, we observe a consistent upward trend in the reward
curves of our Self-Refinement RL (i.e., RefineRL-4B and

to solve increasingly complex competitive programming problems and
adapting to the squared-incentive reward signal. Simultaneously, the
rollout token lengths of our Self-Refinement RL generally exhibit an
increasing trend. This suggests that as the models improve, they learn
to generate more comprehensive solution analyses and engage in more
extensive self-refinement loops to debug and verify their code before
submission, rather than attempting to guess short, likely incorrect
solutions.

## Appendix C Prompts

In this section, we provide the detailed prompt templates used in our
Skeptical-Agent.
Figure [4](#A3.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning")
presents the base system prompt used for initializing the
problem-solving process and generating the initial solution. When the
agent enters the refinement loop, the feedback it receives depends on
the outcome of the local testing. If the solution fails the local test
cases, the agent receives a detailed error report constructed using the
template in
Figure [5](#A3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
which incorporates specific failure reasons (e.g., Wrong Answer, Runtime
Error) as detailed in
Figure [6](#A3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning").
Conversely, if the solution passes the local tests, our Skeptical-Agent
does not immediately accept it. Instead, it triggers a “skeptical”
review using the template in
Figure [7](#A3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ Appendix C Prompts ‣ RefineRL: Advancing Competitive Programming with Self-Refinement Reinforcement Learning"),
forcing the model to self-verify against potential edge cases,
hard-coded cheats, or complexity issues before final submission.

## Appendix D Self-Refinement Example

In this section, we show how our RefineRL-4B-2507 leverages the
Skeptical-Agent to perform self-refinement.

We take the 166th problem from LiveCodeBench v6 as an example. In the
7th round of self-refinement, the model generated a solution that passed
the public test cases but received a Wrong Answer on the private test
cases. However, in the 8th round, the Skeptical-Agent successfully
prompted the model to refine its previous output, resulting in a new
solution that passed all private test cases.
